terms.title: Adobe
terms.text: Sun-dried earth blocks or monolithic earth walls. Common in Mexico for centuries; needs good roof overhangs, foundation capillary break, and detailing for driving rain.

terms.title: Biodigester
terms.text: Anaerobic treatment system that breaks down organic waste and can produce gas for cooking; alternative or complement to septic in rural Mexico where approved.

terms.title: Bioswale / rain garden
terms.text: Vegetated shallow channel or basin that filters runoff and encourages infiltration—useful for roof overflow and road water on site.

terms.title: Blackwater
terms.text: Wastewater from toilets and kitchen grease; requires sealed plumbing, septic or biodigester, or municipal sewer where available. Must meet health codes.

terms.title: Cenote
terms.text: Natural sinkhole exposing groundwater in the Yucatán karst. Ecologically sensitive; regulations protect many. Never assume you can drill or discharge near one without permits.

terms.title: Fideicomiso
terms.text: A bank-held trust allowing non-Mexicans to hold residential property in restricted zones (e.g. within 50 km of coast or 100 km of borders). Not legal advice—verify with a notary.

terms.title: Food forest
terms.text: A layered planting of mostly perennial food and support species (canopy to ground cover) that mimics forest structure, builds soil, and reduces maintenance once established.

terms.title: Greywater
terms.text: Used water from showers, laundry, and sinks (not toilets), redirected to mulch basins or irrigation where law and soil allow. Reduces load on septic or treatment.

terms.title: Karst
terms.text: Limestone geology with rapid infiltration and caves. Pollution reaches groundwater quickly; septic fields and chemicals need extra caution.

terms.title: Maya / Yucatec vernacular
terms.text: Regional patterns: lime or earth mortars, stone or block bases, steep roofs, high ceilings, cross-ventilation, and sometimes local finishes (e.g. chukum-based renders in parts of the peninsula).

terms.title: Passive solar
terms.text: Using sun, shade, and building shape to heat and cool with minimal mechanical energy. In hot-humid Yucatán, emphasis is usually on shade, cross-ventilation, and roof performance more than winter gain.

terms.title: Permaculture
terms.text: Design framework for resilient land use: observe, zone spaces by use frequency, integrate water, plants, animals, and structures. Often overlaps with food forests and keyline ideas.

terms.title: Rainwater harvesting
terms.text: Capturing roof runoff into cisterns or tanks, often with first-flush diversion and filtration for domestic use or irrigation. Yucatán’s seasonal rain makes storage sizing critical.

terms.title: Regenerative agriculture
terms.text: Farming and gardening practices focused on soil organic matter, water retention, and biodiversity—e.g. minimal tillage, cover, integrated animals or mulch—scaled here to homestead and multi-acre land.

terms.title: Regenerative habitat
terms.text: A dwelling and site approach that aims to improve soil, water, and biodiversity over time—not just “less bad” building. Often pairs local materials, passive comfort, rainwater, and perennial plant systems.

terms.title: Swale
terms.text: On-contour ditch and berm to slow runoff and infiltrate water. Useful on sloped lots; on flat karst, infiltration behavior differs—site-specific design matters.

terms.title: Thermal mass
terms.text: Heavy materials (adobe, stone, concrete) that store heat and coolth and release it slowly. Works with—not instead of—insulation, shading, and ventilation in the tropics.
